# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Rationale and pharmacology

Heart failure (HF) is characterised by maladaptive neurohormonal activation, with overactivity of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system counterbalanced—incompletely—by the natriuretic peptide system. Sacubitril/valsartan (formerly LCZ696) is a first-in-class agent that simultaneously blocks the angiotensin II type 1 receptor and inhibits neprilysin, the enzyme that degrades natriuretic peptides, bradykinin and adrenomedullin. Inhibition of neprilysin increases levels of natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin, thus resulting in natriuresis and vasodilatation. [1] The dual mechanism builds on earlier attempts at vasopeptidase inhibition. In the OVERTURE trial, the combined ACE/neprilysin inhibitor omapatrilat was tested against enalapril; the OVERTURE trial demonstrates that omapatrilat reduced morbidity and mortality in patients with moderate-to-severe heart failure but was not more effective than ACE inhibition alone in reducing the risk of a primary clinical event [2]. Concerns about angio-oedema with simultaneous ACE and neprilysin inhibition led to the rational pairing of neprilysin inhibition with an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than an ACE inhibitor [3].

## Pivotal evidence in HFrEF: PARADIGM-HF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the therapeutic value of this approach. In this double-blind trial, 8442 patients with class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of 40% or less were randomly assigned to receive either LCZ696 (at a dose of 200 mg twice daily) or enalapril (at a dose of 10 mg twice daily), in addition to recommended therapy. [4] PARADIGM-HF showed sacubitril/valsartan's superiority over enalapril in reducing cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% [4]. The benefit extended to both modes of cardiovascular death, including sudden death and death from worsening HF [5]. Importantly, the advantage of sacubitril/valsartan over enalapril was consistent irrespective of background therapy [6] and was maintained even among patients who required dose reduction during the trial [7]. Beyond hard endpoints, fewer LCZ696-treated patients required intensification of medical treatment for heart failure or an emergency department visit for worsening heart failure [8], and health-related quality of life was better preserved with sacubitril/valsartan [9].

Several secondary analyses clarified safety and mechanism. In patients receiving a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, severe hyperkalemia was more common in patients randomly assigned to enalapril than to sacubitril/valsartan, suggesting MRAs can be used more safely with ARNI [10]. Sacubitril/valsartan also modestly improved glycaemic control in patients with diabetes [11]. Mechanistically, the PROVE-HF study demonstrated that reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was weakly yet significantly correlated with improvements in markers of cardiac volume and function at 12 months, supporting reverse cardiac remodelling as a contributor to clinical benefit [12,13].

## Initiation in and after hospitalisation

Because PARADIGM-HF enrolled stable outpatients, dedicated trials addressed in-hospital initiation. PIONEER-HF was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial of in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril in patients stabilized during hospitalization for acute decompensated HF. [14] The time-averaged reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was significantly greater in the sacubitril-valsartan group than the enalapril group, with similar rates of worsening renal function, hyperkalaemia, hypotension and angio-oedema [14]. The open-label TRANSITION study likewise supported initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in haemodynamically stabilised heart failure patients in hospital or early after discharge [15], and a de novo HF subgroup analysis confirmed feasibility in newly diagnosed patients [16].

## Across the ejection fraction spectrum

Whether benefit extends beyond reduced ejection fraction has been a central question. In PARAGON-HF, sacubitril–valsartan did not result in a significantly lower rate of total hospitalizations for heart failure and death from cardiovascular causes among patients with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 45% or higher. [17] However, the primary endpoint was narrowly missed (HR 0.87, CI 0.75–1.01; P = 0.059), and prespecified subgroups suggested benefit in those with lower ejection fraction and in women [17,18]. A pooled analysis across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF found that the therapeutic effects of sacubitril/valsartan, compared with a RAS inhibitor alone, vary by LVEF, with treatment benefits, particularly for heart failure hospitalization, that appear to extend to patients with heart failure and mildly reduced ejection fraction [19]. Renal outcomes were also more favourable with ARNI in PARAGON-HF [20]. The PARAGLIDE-HF trial subsequently examined ARNI after a worsening HF event in EF >40%; together with pooled analyses, these data suggest that combined angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibition is likely more effective than angiotensin receptor blockade alone in patients with HF and EF >40%, with a larger benefit when EF is below normal [21,22].

## Guideline recommendations and practical considerations

Contemporary guidelines incorporate these findings. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline addresses the entire spectrum of HF function with new treatment strategies including ARNI [23,24], and the 2021 ESC guidelines provide parallel recommendations for chronic HF [25,26]. Sacubitril/valsartan is now positioned, alongside beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors, as foundational therapy for HFrEF [23,25]. In practice, ARNI should be initiated after a washout from ACE inhibitors to mitigate angio-oedema risk, with attention to hypotension and renal function; real-world registries show that uptake and target-dose attainment remain suboptimal [27]. Lower-dose strata still derive benefit [7,28], and titration regimens have been studied to improve tolerability [29]. The 2023 PARAGLIDE-HF data and ongoing analyses continue to refine patient selection across the EF and acuity spectrum [22,30].

## Conclusion

Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibition represents a major therapeutic advance for HFrEF, reducing mortality and hospitalisation beyond ACE inhibition, with emerging—if more modest—benefits in patients with mildly reduced and preserved ejection fraction. Its established efficacy, demonstrable reverse remodelling, safety when initiated in or shortly after hospitalisation, and prominent place in international guidelines together justify its role as a cornerstone of modern HF pharmacotherapy.
